Ovidrel: injection-site pain 16.2% (ovulation induction study); application site disorders 14.6%
Ovidrel: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache and mild or moderate OHSS listed as common (more than 1 in 100)
warnings: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) can be triggered by hCG; patients are followed for at least two weeks after hCG. Ovidrel monograph: maximum severity at 7 to 10 days; patient leaflet gives incidence usually under 3%; independent risk factors include age under 30 and lean body mass
Multiple pregnancy: increased risk with ovulation induction (Ovidrel trial: 2 of 15 live deliveries, 13.3%, were multiple births)
Thromboembolic events reported both with and separate from OHSS (Pregnyl); Ovidrel lists thromboembolism as very rare (1/10,000)
Ectopic pregnancy, pregnancy loss and possibly congenital malformations are more frequent with assisted reproduction; ovarian torsion reported after hCG
Prepubertal boys: use cautiously to avoid premature epiphyseal closure or precocious sexual development
Men: hCG increases androgen production
Heart or kidney disease, epilepsy, migraine or asthma (or a history of them): close supervision, as aggravation or recurrence may occur
Pregnancy tests: hCG may interfere for up to ten days with serum/urinary hCG tests
Not for weight loss: Pregnyl and Fresenius Kabi monographs state hCG has not been shown effective for obesity and should not be used for body weight reduction
Male uses outside the listed indications are not in the Canadian monographs

interactions: Pregnyl: interactions not studied; interactions with commonly used medicines cannot be excluded
Ovidrel: no clinically significant drug interactions reported during hCG therapy

specialPopulations: Pregnancy: Pregnyl not used after pregnancy is established; Ovidrel contraindicated in pregnancy
Breastfeeding: Pregnyl must not be used during lactation; Ovidrel not indicated during breastfeeding
Children: Pregnyl and Fresenius Kabi list prepubertal cryptorchidism; Ovidrel is only for female patients of reproductive age

Omnitrope: 2-8 C, do not freeze, in original package to protect from light. Saizen 5 mg vial: room temperature not above 25 C in original package. Saizen cartridges: 2-8 C, do not freeze. Norditropin FlexPro: 2-8 C, do not freeze, avoid direct light.

Saizen cartridges: 2-8 C up to 28 days, of which no more than 7 days at room temperature (not above 25 C); discard after 28 days or if more than 7 days out of the refrigerator. Saizen vial: with bacteriostatic water 2-8 C up to 14 days; with water for injection, use within 3 hours. Norditropin FlexPro: refrigerated and used within 4 weeks, OR up to 3 weeks at not more than 25 C.

Fluid retention may occur during replacement in adults
Carpal tunnel syndrome appears more frequent in patients over 40 (2% of 3,031 patients in extension studies); Saizen advises dose reduction, then stopping if symptoms persist
Acute critical illness: in trials mortality was 42% with somatropin vs 19% placebo; such patients should not be treated
Prader-Willi syndrome: fatalities reported in children with severe obesity, respiratory impairment, sleep apnea or respiratory infection
Thyroid and adrenal: may unmask hypothyroidism (check thyroid at least annually) and central hypoadrenalism; optimise corticosteroid replacement before starting
Norditropin monograph also lists pancreatitis in children
contraindications: Any evidence of active neoplasia; intracranial lesions must be inactive and antitumour therapy complete
Active proliferative or severe non-proliferative (preproliferative) diabetic retinopathy
Acute critical illness from complications after open heart or abdominal surgery, multiple accidental trauma, or acute respiratory failure
Growth promotion in children with closed (fused) epiphyses
Hypersensitivity to somatropin or any ingredient (for example metacresol in Genotropin GoQuick)
Prader-Willi syndrome with severe obesity, upper airway obstruction or sleep apnea, or severe respiratory impairment
Omnitrope 5 mg/1.5 mL (benzyl alcohol): not for newborns or people sensitive to benzyl alcohol
Norditropin: renal transplantation
Saizen: not recommended during pregnancy and lactation
interactions: Glucocorticoids: monitor serum cortisol; replacement or stress doses may need adjustment
Oral estrogens: women on oral estrogen may be under-treated and need higher doses
Insulin and other diabetes medicines: may need adjustment because somatropin can reduce insulin sensitivity
Thyroid: increased T4-to-T3 conversion; may unmask hypothyroidism
Drugs cleared by CYP450 (corticosteroids, sex steroids, anticonvulsants, cyclosporine): clearance may change; careful monitoring advised
specialPopulations: Women, especially on oral estrogen: may need higher doses
Older adults: lower starting dose and smaller increments considered; requirements fall with age
Pregnancy: Omnitrope only if benefits clearly outweigh risks; Saizen not recommended
Breastfeeding: no data on passage into milk (Omnitrope); Saizen not recommended
Children: weight-based dosing by a specialist; Norditropin is pediatric only in Canada
wada: Prohibited at all times (in and out of competition): S2.2.3 Growth hormone (GH), its analogues and fragments (2026 List; 2027 List in force 2027-01-01 keeps GH under S2).

names.generic: long-acting growth hormone (somapacitan, somatrogon; lonapegsomatropin not in Canada)

statusDetail.healthCanada: Sogroya (somapacitan, Novo Nordisk): 3 pens marketed since 2023-11-27; current monograph authorizes adults with GHD and children with growth failure. Ngenla (somatrogon, Pfizer): 2 pens marketed since 2022-02-22; pediatric only (not indicated in adults). Skytrofa (lonapegsomatropin): no DPD record found.
statusDetail.fda: Sogroya (somapacitan-beco): initial US approval 2020; adults with GHD and children 2.5 years and older (label revised 2/2026). Ngenla (somatrogon-ghla): initial US approval 2023; children 3 years and older. Skytrofa (lonapegsomatropin-tcgd): initial US approval 2021; children 1 year and older weighing at least 11.5 kg, and adults with GHD (label revised 9/2025).
statusDetail.other: Skytrofa (lonapegsomatropin) is approved in the US (FDA label on DailyMed) but has no Health Canada DPD record as of 2026-11-17, so it is not listed in products.

indications: Sogroya: replacement of endogenous growth hormone in adults with growth hormone deficiency; long-term treatment of children with growth failure due to inadequate endogenous growth hormone (efficacy and safety not established under 2.5 years)

Ngenla: long-term treatment of pediatric patients with growth failure due to inadequate secretion of endogenous growth hormone (established at 3 to 11 years; limited data at 12 to under 18; not established under 3); "NGENLA is not indicated for use in adults"
Neither Canadian monograph lists anti-aging, body composition or athletic use
mechanism: Long-acting growth hormone analogues given once weekly instead of daily; IGF-I levels are used to guide dosing.

products.device: Multidose disposable prefilled pen: 5 mg pen (teal) doses 0.025-2 mg in 0.025 mg steps; 10 mg pen (yellow) 0.05-4 mg in 0.05 mg steps; 15 mg pen (rubine red) 0.1-8 mg in 0.1 mg steps; NovoFine needles up to 8 mm sold separately

Single-patient disposable prefilled pen: 24 mg pen (lilac) dials 0.2 mg steps, max 12 mg per injection; 60 mg pen (blue) dials 0.5 mg steps, max 30 mg per injection; needles up to 8 mm sold separately

deviceNotes: Sogroya: single-person pen; the cartridge must not be refilled

Ngenla: new sterile needle for each injection; prime each new pen (0.4 mg on the 24 mg pen, 1.0 mg on the 60 mg pen); doses above the per-injection maximum need more than one injection at different sites
Ngenla: rotate the injection site each week

doseInfo.population: Adults with growth hormone deficiency (Sogroya)
doseInfo.regimen: Once weekly. Starting dose 1.5 mg (age 18 to under 60), 1.0 mg (60 and older), 2.0 mg (women on oral estrogen, any age). Increase gradually every 2 to 4 weeks in steps of 0.5 mg to 1.5 mg based on clinical response and adverse reactions, aiming for IGF-I SDS within the age-adjusted upper reference range within 12 months. IGF-I sample drawn 3-4 days after dosing.
doseInfo.maxDose: 8 mg once weekly
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Switching from daily GH: last daily dose the day before, or at least 8 hours before, the first weekly dose

doseInfo.population: Children with growth failure due to GH deficiency (Sogroya): weight-based, set by a specialist
doseInfo.regimen: 0.16 mg/kg body weight once weekly (treatment-naive or switching from daily somatropin); may be lowered if IGF-I SDS repeatedly above +2
doseInfo.maxDose: Doses above 0.16 mg/kg/week have not been studied
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Not established under 2.5 years

doseInfo.population: Children with growth failure due to GH deficiency (Ngenla): weight-based, set by a specialist
doseInfo.regimen: "The recommended dose is 0.66 mg/kg body weight administered once weekly by subcutaneous (SC) injection." Switching from daily GH: start the day after the last daily injection. IGF-1 "samples should always be drawn 4 days after the prior dose"; if IGF-1 exceeds the mean by more than 2 SDS, reduce the dose by 15%.
doseInfo.maxDose: "Doses of NGENLA higher than 0.66 mg/kg body weight/week have not been studied."
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Pediatric only in Canada

missedDose.text: Sogroya: "inject SOGROYA upon discovery as soon as possible within 3 days after the missed dose, and then resume their usual once-weekly dosing schedule. If more than 3 days have passed, the dose should be skipped, and the next dose should be administered on the regularly scheduled day." Day may be changed if "the time between two doses is at least 4 days (96 hours)". Ngenla: "administer NGENLA as soon as possible within 3 days after the missed dose. If more than 3 days have passed, skip the missed dose and administer the next dose on the regularly scheduled day." Day may be changed if "the time between 2 doses is at least 3 days (>72 hours)". Top-level minHoursBetweenDoses uses the stricter Sogroya value; see byProduct.

storage.unopened: Sogroya: refrigerate at 2-8 C until expiry; may be kept at room temperature up to 30 C for a total of 72 hours (unopened or in use); discard if kept above 30 C. Ngenla: refrigerate at 2-8 C, do not freeze, keep in carton to protect from light.
storage.inUse: Sogroya: refrigerated (2-8 C) up to 6 weeks after first use, within the same 72-hour total room-temperature allowance. Ngenla: refrigerated (2-8 C) for a single period of up to 28 days from first use and a maximum of 5 uses; may be at room temperature (no more than 32 C) for a maximum of 2 hours before each injection.

commonSideEffects: Sogroya adults: headache 12%, arthralgia 7%, fatigue 6%, peripheral oedema 4%
Sogroya children: headache 12%, hypothyroidism 5%, injection site reactions 5%, peripheral edema 3%
Ngenla children (vs daily somatropin): injection site reactions 43.1% vs 25.2%, injection site pain 39.4% vs 25.2%, headache 16.5% vs 21.7%, fever 16.5% vs 13.9%, hypothyroidism 6.4% vs 2.6%
warnings: Acute critical illness: increased mortality reported with GH; discontinue or consider discontinuing
Neoplasms: risk of tumour progression and second neoplasms (childhood cancer survivors); malignant change in pre-existing nevi
Intracranial hypertension: stop if papilledema or fundoscopic signs occur
Glucose: reduced insulin sensitivity, hyperglycemia or new-onset type 2 diabetes; monitor glucose
Adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism may be unmasked; monitor
Fluid retention (Sogroya), usually transient and dose-dependent
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis and scoliosis progression in children; evaluate a new limp or hip or knee pain
Prader-Willi syndrome: deaths reported with risk factors (Ngenla not studied in this population)
Pancreatitis, serious hypersensitivity reactions, lipoatrophy or lipohypertrophy (rotate sites)
Ngenla: very rare myositis, possibly linked to the preservative metacresol
contraindications: Any evidence of active neoplasm or malignancy (Sogroya: intracranial tumours must be inactive and treatment complete)
Growth promotion in children with closed epiphyses
Acute critical illness after open heart or abdominal surgery, multiple accidental trauma, or acute respiratory failure
Hypersensitivity to the drug or any ingredient
Sogroya: children with Prader-Willi syndrome who are severely obese or have severe respiratory impairment
interactions: Glucocorticoids: replacement or stress doses may need to increase; monitor
Oral estrogen may reduce the IGF-I response; higher doses may be needed (Ngenla: weekly maximum still applies)
Insulin and other diabetes medicines may need dose adjustment
Drugs metabolised by CYP450 (corticosteroids, sex steroids, anticonvulsants, cyclosporine): clearance may change
Thyroid hormone: thyroid function monitored; untreated hypothyroidism may blunt response
Sogroya: no formal drug interaction studies performed
specialPopulations: Older adults (Sogroya): lower starting dose of 1.0 mg weekly at 60 and older
Women on oral estrogen (Sogroya): starting dose 2.0 mg weekly
Pregnancy (Sogroya): no human data; skeletal malformations in rats only at 18 mg/kg/day
Breastfeeding (Sogroya): no data on presence in human milk; risk cannot be excluded
Children: Sogroya from 2.5 years; Ngenla established at 3 to 11 years, limited data 12 to under 18
wada: Prohibited at all times (in and out of competition): S2.2.3 names growth hormone analogues lonapegsomatropin, somapacitan and somatrogon (2026 List; 2027 List in force 2027-01-01 keeps GH under S2).
evidenceLevel: Approved, extensive use (for the labelled indications)

indications: Testosterone replacement therapy in adult males for conditions associated with a deficiency or absence of endogenous testosterone (hypogonadism) (both marketed monographs)
Hikma enanthate monograph: hypogonadism confirmed by two separate morning testosterone assays; not indicated in women; not indicated under 18 (safety and efficacy not established)

No separate delayed-puberty indication in either monograph; the enanthate monograph gives a starting regimen for prepubertal-onset hypogonadism and the cypionate monograph advises caution in males with hypogonadism causing delayed puberty
mechanism: Long-acting testosterone ester in oil, given by deep intramuscular injection; replaces testosterone the body is not making.

Not verified (monograph not fetched)

deviceNotes: Cypionate (Taro): intramuscular use only, not for intravenous use; vial stopper not made with natural rubber latex
Enanthate (Hikma): injected deeply into the gluteal muscle; vial stopper not made with natural rubber latex

doseInfo.population: Adult hypogonadal males: testosterone cypionate (Taro-Testosterone Cypionate)
doseInfo.regimen: 200 mg intramuscularly every two weeks
doseInfo.maxDose: 400 mg per month
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Replacement therapy; serum testosterone monitored on a regular basis

doseInfo.population: Adult hypogonadal males: testosterone enanthate (Hikma)
doseInfo.regimen: Usual dose 100 to 400 mg every four weeks. The monograph also cites 50 to 100 mg every 7 to 10 days for complete replacement, and 100 to 150 mg every 2 weeks as 'a reasonable compromise'; 300 mg every 3 weeks is described as generally inadequate for a consistent response.
doseInfo.maxDose: No explicit maximum; 'In general, total doses above 400 mg per month are not required'; injections more often than every two weeks are rarely indicated
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Deep intramuscular injection into the gluteal muscle

doseInfo.maxDose: As for adult replacement
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Enanthate monograph also lists 50 to 100 mg every 2 weeks as an initial regimen in men with benign prostatic hypertrophy

missedDose.text: Both monographs state a missed dose is given as soon as possible; if it is almost time for the next dose, the missed dose is skipped and the regular schedule resumed; doses are not doubled. No hour cut-off is given.

storage.unopened: Cypionate (Taro): room temperature 15 to 30 C, protect from light. Enanthate (Hikma): controlled room temperature 15 to 30 C.

commonSideEffects: No percentages given: the enanthate monograph states frequencies cannot be reliably estimated and clinical-trial data are not available

Listed androgen reactions: injection-site inflammation and pain; acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, male-pattern baldness; gynecomastia; prolonged erections; oligospermia; libido changes, headache, anxiety, depression, paresthesia; nausea; fluid and electrolyte retention; polycythemia; liver test changes and cholestatic jaundice; hypersensitivity
Post-market reports include pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, hypertension and chorioretinopathy
warnings: Neither marketed injection monograph has a boxed Serious Warnings section
Polycythemia: hemoglobin and hematocrit should be checked periodically; no hematocrit cut-off is stated
Blood pressure: testosterone may increase blood pressure; use with caution in hypertension
Cardiovascular: post-market studies suggest increased risk of serious cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke
Venous thromboembolism: pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis appear in the post-market adverse reaction tables (no separate narrative warning in these two monographs)

Abuse and dependence: testosterone has been abused, typically at doses higher than recommended; anabolic steroid abuse can cause serious psychiatric and cardiovascular effects, which may be fatal; supratherapeutic use may cause withdrawal symptoms lasting weeks or months (cypionate); 'habituation (dependence)' listed (enanthate)

Suppression of own production and sperm: endogenous testosterone release may be inhibited through feedback inhibition of pituitary LH, and spermatogenesis may be suppressed through feedback inhibition of FSH (enanthate monograph); oligospermia may occur after prolonged administration or excessive dosage (both)
Edema, with or without congestive heart failure, may be a serious complication
Liver: peliosis hepatis can be life-threatening or fatal; hepatic adenomas reported
Sleep apnea may be potentiated, particularly with obesity or chronic lung disease
Prostate: increased risk of prostatic hyperplasia and prostatic carcinoma (enanthate monograph)
Monitoring listed: serum testosterone on a regular basis; hemoglobin and hematocrit; PSA and digital rectal exam; lipid profile; liver function tests; diabetics followed carefully
contraindications: Known or suspected carcinoma of the prostate or breast in men
Not indicated in women; enanthate monograph: contraindicated in women, including pregnant or nursing women
Known hypersensitivity to any ingredient
interactions: Oral anticoagulants: androgens may increase sensitivity; anticoagulant dose may need reduction and close monitoring when androgens are started or stopped
Insulin and other diabetes medicines: androgens may decrease blood glucose and insulin requirements
ACTH or corticosteroids: may enhance edema formation
Propranolol: testosterone cypionate increased propranolol clearance in most men tested (enanthate monograph)
Thyroid tests: androgens may decrease thyroxine-binding globulin
Herbal products may interfere with steroid metabolism and lower plasma testosterone
specialPopulations: Women: not indicated (enanthate: contraindicated, including pregnancy and nursing)
Under 18: not indicated (safety and efficacy not established)
Over 65: limited controlled data
Diabetes: glucose and insulin needs may change
wada: Prohibited at all times (in- and out-of-competition): testosterone is listed under S1 Anabolic Agents on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List (in effect 1 January 2026).

Wait before showering or bathing: at least 1 hour for AndroGel and Taro gel (AndroGel patient information also says 1 hour before swimming); at least 2 hours for Testim

commonSideEffects: AndroGel: enlarged prostate 11.9% (most frequent adverse reaction); in the 180-day controlled trial acne 1 to 8%, lab abnormalities 3 to 6%, application-site reactions 3 to 5%, prostate disorders 3 to 5%; in the 3-year extension enlarged prostate 11.7%, application-site reactions 5.6%, acne 3.1%; serum PSA increases in about 18% of patients
Testim 1% (clinical trials, Table 1): increased PSA 4.3%, application-site erythema 4.1%, increased hematocrit 3.9%, increased hemoglobin 3.7%
Post-market reports include pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis (Testim)
warnings: Boxed Serious Warning (AndroGel, Taro-Testosterone Gel): secondary exposure. Virilization has been reported in children secondarily exposed to testosterone, including AndroGel; children should avoid contact with unwashed or unclothed application sites; patients should strictly follow the instructions for use

Testim 1% serious warning: gel can transfer to another person through skin-to-skin contact; signs of puberty reported in exposed children; children kept away from unwashed or unclothed application sites and from unwashed clothing or fabrics exposed to the gel

Transfer to women: secondary exposure can occur in women and children; if a woman's skin contacts the site, the area is washed immediately with soap and water; pregnant and nursing women should avoid skin contact with application sites
Polycythemia: hemoglobin and hematocrit checked periodically; dose adjustment or stopping until values normalize may be needed (no hematocrit cut-off stated)
Blood pressure: testosterone may increase blood pressure; caution in hypertension
Cardiovascular: post-market studies suggest increased risk of serious cardiovascular events
Venous thromboembolism: caution with thrombophilia or risk factors for VTE; VTE including DVT and PE listed (AndroGel)

Controlled substance: the AndroGel monograph describes testosterone as 'a Schedule G controlled substance as defined by the Food and Drugs Act' (DPD lists CDSA IV); detailed abuse and dependence wording was not extracted from the gel monographs

Suppression of sperm production: with large doses of exogenous androgens, including AndroGel, spermatogenesis may be reversibly suppressed through feedback inhibition of FSH; Testim: oligospermia may occur after prolonged administration or excessive dosage
Monitoring listed: serum testosterone after starting (Testim: about 7 to 14 days); hemoglobin and hematocrit; PSA and digital rectal exam (AndroGel)
contraindications: Known or suspected carcinoma of the prostate or breast in men
Not indicated in women; pregnant and nursing women should avoid skin contact with application sites
Known hypersensitivity to testosterone or any ingredient
interactions: Oral anticoagulants: androgens may increase sensitivity
Insulin and other diabetes medicines: dose reduction may be needed
Corticosteroids: may enhance edema formation
Propranolol: increased clearance seen with injectable testosterone; unknown whether it applies to AndroGel
specialPopulations: Women: not indicated; pregnant and nursing women avoid contact with application sites
Children: not indicated under 18; risk of virilization from secondary exposure
wada: Prohibited at all times (in- and out-of-competition): testosterone is listed under S1 Anabolic Agents on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List (in effect 1 January 2026).

indications: Testosterone replacement therapy in adult males for conditions associated with a deficiency or absence of endogenous testosterone (hypogonadism) (Taro-Testosterone, Kyzatrex)
Kyzatrex: deficiency confirmed by two separate morning biochemical assays before starting
Not indicated in women or under 18 (Taro-Testosterone)
mechanism: Oral testosterone ester (undecanoate) taken twice daily with a meal; the Kyzatrex monograph states dietary fat enhances its absorption.

doseInfo.population: Adult hypogonadal males: Taro-Testosterone 40 mg capsules
doseInfo.regimen: Initial 120 to 160 mg daily, divided into two doses (morning and evening), for 2 to 3 weeks; then 40 to 120 mg daily based on testosterone levels and/or clinical effect
doseInfo.maxDose: 160 mg daily (top of the initial range)
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Bioavailable or calculated free testosterone measured about 5 hours after a capsule dose

doseInfo.population: Adult hypogonadal males: Kyzatrex
doseInfo.regimen: Start 200 mg twice daily (morning and evening) with meals. Serum testosterone checked 7 days after starting or after any dose change, 3 to 5 hours after the morning dose: below 460 ng/dL the dose is stepped up; 460 to 971 ng/dL no change; above 971 ng/dL the dose is stepped down; at the lowest step (100 mg once daily in the morning) treatment is discontinued if still above 971 ng/dL
doseInfo.maxDose: 400 mg twice daily (minimum 100 mg once daily in the morning)
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Titration table in the fetched PDF text is partly garbled; step sizes between 100 and 400 mg recorded as open question

missedDose.text: Taro-Testosterone and Kyzatrex: the missed dose is not made up; the next dose is taken at the usual scheduled time; no double dose.

storage.unopened: Taro-Testosterone: 15 to 30 C, protected from light and moisture, not refrigerated, blister kept in the outer carton. Kyzatrex: 20 to 25 C in the original bottle, protected from light and moisture.

commonSideEffects: Kyzatrex (pooled Phase 3, n=296, treatment-related): any 22.3%; hypertension 2.7%; hemoglobin increased 2.4%; PSA increased 1.7%; by system: investigations 7.4%, gastrointestinal 3.7%, psychiatric 3.0%, reproductive/breast 2.7%, skin 2.7%
Kyzatrex blood pressure: mean increase 1.7/0.6 mm Hg at 4 months; 3.4/0.7 mm Hg in patients on antihypertensives
Taro-Testosterone: no frequencies given; post-market listings include polycythemia, hypertension, gynecomastia, priapism, hepatic neoplasms, thromboembolic events
warnings: Neither monograph has a boxed Serious Warnings section (as fetched)
Blood pressure: testosterone may increase blood pressure (Taro-Testosterone: caution in hypertension; Kyzatrex: not recommended in uncontrolled hypertension)
Cardiovascular: post-market studies suggest increased risk of serious cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke
Polycythemia: hemoglobin and hematocrit checked periodically in long-term therapy; no hematocrit cut-off stated
Venous thromboembolism: caution with thrombophilia or VTE risk factors; continuing after a first thrombotic event should be carefully evaluated (Kyzatrex)
Abuse and dependence: testosterone abuse may result in dependence and withdrawal symptoms; abuse, often with other anabolic steroids, can cause serious cardiovascular, hepatic and psychiatric events

Suppression of own production and sperm: endogenous testosterone release may be inhibited through feedback inhibition of pituitary LH, and with large doses spermatogenesis may be suppressed (Kyzatrex); at large doses spermatogenesis may be suppressed through feedback on FSH (Taro-Testosterone); oligospermia may occur after prolonged administration or excessive dosage (both)
Monitoring listed: serum testosterone (timing per product above); hemoglobin and hematocrit; PSA and digital rectal exam; lipid profile; liver function tests; diabetics monitored closely
contraindications: Known or suspected carcinoma of the prostate or breast in men
Not indicated in women
Known hypersensitivity to any ingredient
interactions: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin): androgens may increase sensitivity; INR and prothrombin time monitored
Insulin and oral diabetes medicines: blood glucose and insulin requirements may decrease
ACTH or corticosteroids: may enhance edema
Cyclosporine: may be potentiated with increased risk of kidney toxicity (Kyzatrex)
Medicines that raise blood pressure (some prescription, pain and cold medicines) may add to the increase (Kyzatrex)
St. John's Wort may decrease plasma testosterone; propranolol interaction reported with injectable testosterone
nutritionNotes: Taro-Testosterone and Kyzatrex 'must be taken with a meal' and swallowed without chewing; Kyzatrex monograph explains fat enhances its absorption
specialPopulations: Women: not indicated
Under 18: not indicated (Taro-Testosterone)
Older adults: limited data (Taro-Testosterone)
Diabetes: glucose and insulin needs may change
wada: Prohibited at all times (in- and out-of-competition): testosterone is listed under S1 Anabolic Agents on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List (in effect 1 January 2026).
